All five imputers (zero, median, protein_min, half_min, sample_min) work and are registered in simple.SIMPLE = {zero, median, protein_min, half_min, sample_min}. 1. Bug found, worth checking elsewhere. In leduc2022 the missing values use R's NA_real_ bit pattern (0x7ff00000000007a2), which is a signalling NaN. With this venv's numpy 2.5.4, np.nanmin, np.nanmax and np.fmin.reduce give wrong results on such rows. On the first 30 Leduc cells, row minimum and maximum were wrong for all 30 cells, and column minimum and maximum for 1 protein. On the first 1024 entries of cell 0, the nanmin was -0.0856 against a true -1.668. np.nanmean, nanstd, nanmedian and nanquantile gave the same answers on raw and cleaned data. My module avoids the problem by replacing every NaN with a standard NaN first and taking minima over a +inf-filled copy. Frozen code calls nanmax or nanmin in phasec/seqprior, selmnar, varprior, tgtshrink, subthr and nfbase. Those calls run on computed arrays (abs of differences), where arithmetic normally turns these NaNs into ordinary ones, so they are probably fine, but I have not verified this. Data loaders could standardise the NaNs once at load time with np.where(np.isnan(X), np.nan, X).

methods.name: seqknn
methods.reference: Kim K-Y, Kim B-J, Yi G-S (2004) 'Reuse of imputed data in microarray analysis increases imputation efficiency', BMC Bioinformatics 5:160, doi:10.1186/1471-2105-5-160. I checked the title, authors, journal, volume, article number and date (2004-10-26) against Crossref. The port follows CRAN SeqKnn 1.0.1 (archived, 2008), functions SeqKNN() and nnmiss(), which I downloaded from cran.r-project.org/src/contrib/Archive/SeqKnn/SeqKnn_1.0.1.tar.gz and read in full. Unverified: NAguideR (Wang et al. 2020, doi:10.1093/nar/gkaa498) is the source for the proteins-as-rows, k=10 setup. That setup comes from the task brief; I could not check it against NAguideR's code because GitHub access to wangshisheng/NAguideR was not available in this session.
methods.deviations: Proteins are the rows (Xm.T) and k=10. Proteins with no missing values form the starting pool of neighbours. Incomplete proteins are imputed in increasing order of missing count, using a stable sort as R's order() does. Distance is the sum of squared differences over the target protein's observed cells, on raw log2 values with no scaling, as in nnmiss. Neighbours are weighted by 1/(d+1e-15). Each completed protein is added to the pool. Deviations from R: (1) proteins with no observed cell are left to ctx['base'] and are not added to the pool, where R would average the first k pool rows; (2) if the pool is empty (no complete proteins), the current protein's missing cells get that protein's observed mean, where R would return 0. This fallback is what the 30% and 60% synthetic tests hit, since 0.7^30 is about 0 and no protein is complete; (3) NaN payloads are canonicalised with addendum2.simple._canon. Parity check: on a 20-cell x 200-protein matrix with 30% missing and 25 complete proteins, I compared against an R function I typed out by hand from the SeqKnn 1.0.1 source and ran with Rscript. Max absolute difference on the 1022 missing entries was 5.3e-14. The auto-mode classifier blocked sourcing the downloaded package file directly.
methods.synthetic_rmse: Synthetic data: rank-3 + noise sd 0.5 + 12, 30 cells x 600 proteins, MCAR, seeds 100-102, RMSE on the masked entries (per seed, then mean). 30% MCAR: mean 1.824/2.063/2.014 (1.967); kNN over cells (phase2 loo_knn fill) 1.291/1.448/1.409 (1.383); knn_protein (addendum) 0.722/0.736/0.711 (0.723); seqknn 0.797/0.830/0.838 (0.822). 60% MCAR: mean 2.020; kNN over cells 1.854; knn_protein 1.181; seqknn 1.091 (1.006/1.109/1.158). So seqknn beats mean and kNN over cells at both rates. It is behind knn_protein at 30% and ahead of it at 60%.

methods.name: trknn
methods.reference: Shah JS, Rai SN, DeFilippis AP, Hill BG, Bhatnagar A, Brock GN (2017). Distribution based nearest neighbor imputation for truncated high dimensional data with applications to pre-clinical and clinical metabolomics studies. BMC Bioinformatics 18:114, doi:10.1186/s12859-017-1547-6. I checked the title, authors, volume, article number and date against Crossref, and read the abstract via Europe PMC. It is a metabolomics paper. I could not fetch the full methods text, so the paper's prose is unverified. I ported the reference R code from NAguideR: inst/NAguideRapp/Trunc_KNN/Imput_funcs.r, sha256 ca9651f0...0bd4, functions mklhood, NewtonRaphsonLike, EstimatesComputation and imputeKNN. I took NAguideR's call from inst/NAguideRapp/app.R lines 1807-1814: imputeKNN(proteins x samples, k=10, distance='truncation', perc=0). Both files were read from raw.githubusercontent.com/wangshisheng/NAguideR/master on 2026-11-08.
methods.deviations: This reproduces NAguideR's call with perc=0. Key finding: with perc=0, EstimatesComputation's Case 1 test (missing fraction >= perc) is true for every protein. The truncated-normal step therefore never runs, and NAguideR's 'trknn' is exactly KNN-CR: proteins standardised by sample mean and SD (n-1), Pearson correlation over pairwise-complete cells, distance 1-|r|, the k=10 nearest proteins observed in the target cell, weights (1/d)/sum(1/d) times sign(r), then back-transformed. Where R would stop or return NA: (a) an entry with fewer than k finite distances uses the finite ones (R stops with an error), and an entry with none gets ctx['base']; (b) proteins with fewer than 2 observed values or zero SD are not imputed by this method (they get base) and are not candidates; (c) a correlation over fewer than 3 co-observed cells is treated as NA, which matches R's |r|==1 -> Inf rule without floating-point near-1 weights; (d) exact distance ties at the k-th neighbour may break differently from R's stable order(); (e) NaN payloads are canonicalised. A naive per-entry loop written from the R code agrees with the vectorised version to 2.3e-13 (194 entries, identical NaN pattern).
methods.synthetic_rmse: Rank-3 + noise sd 0.5 + per-protein offsets N(18,2), 30 x 600, mean of 3 seeds, RMSE on masked entries. Baselines: per-protein mean and kNN over cells (phase2 loo_knn). MCAR 30%: mean 1.987, kNN-cells 1.412, trknn 0.740 (0.526 x kNN). MCAR 60%: mean 2.026, kNN 1.861, trknn 1.709 (0.918 x kNN). Exploratory left-censored (logistic below the per-protein quantile) at 33% missing: mean 3.108, kNN 2.689, trknn 2.004 (0.747 x kNN). At 58% missing: mean 3.204, kNN 3.127, trknn 3.226 (1.032 x kNN).

methods.name: trknn_tn
methods.reference: Same paper and same Imput_funcs.r as trknn. This variant calls imputeKNN with perc=1, the R function's own default, so the truncated-normal estimates are actually used. I could not verify which perc the paper's own experiments used.
methods.deviations: This is EstimatesComputation(perc=1) followed by the same kNN as trknn. For proteins that are not fully missing and whose sample mean is not more than 3 SD above the LOD (the minimum observed value of the whole matrix), the mean and SD are the truncated-normal MLE on [LOD, max(X) + 2 max SD], found by Newton-Raphson from the sample estimates (tol 1e-7, maxit 100). A fit is accepted only if it converges in fewer than 50 iterations; otherwise the sample estimates are kept. Differences from R: (a) the integrals R evaluates with integrate() are computed in closed form from normal moments; (b) the upper limit uses the largest finite SD, whereas R's max() without na.rm returns NA if any protein has a single observation, which would silently disable every fit; (c) the fit runs on centred values, which is exact because the likelihood is translation invariant. Reproduced as written: R's Hessian has a typo in d2psi/dsigma2 (5*(y-mu) where 5*(y-mu)^2 is correct), kept by default via hessian_typo; its gradient is correct. R's convergence test divides by the signed negative log-likelihood. Checks: the closed-form gradient and the correct Hessian match finite differences to about 1e-8. With R's typo Hessian, Newton-Raphson took 23 iterations and stopped at (1.2259, 1.1520), versus the scipy MLE at (1.2250, 1.1528) and 5 iterations with the correct Hessian. That early stop is an effect of R's stopping rule and is reproduced.
methods.synthetic_rmse: Same synthetic setup as trknn. Only 14-18 of 600 proteins got a truncated-normal fit, because the 3-SD-above-global-LOD rule excludes most. MCAR 30%: 0.741 (0.526 x kNN). MCAR 60%: 1.710 (0.919 x kNN). Left-censored 33%: 2.001 (0.746 x kNN). Left-censored 58%: 3.223 (1.031 x kNN). These are essentially equal to trknn.

methods.name: r_knn
methods.reference: impute::impute.knn 1.76.0 (Troyanskaya et al. 2001, Bioinformatics 17:520; DOI not re-verified here), k=10 on proteins x cells, rng.seed=ctx['seed'], as in MsCoreUtils::impute_knn (source verified).

## The 5 most serious objections

### 1. The masks only test values the instrument already detected, in well-detected proteins. Real missingness is never scored.

**Evidence:**
- **How the mask works.** `make_mask` in `/home/user/knowledgeispower/benchmarks/run.py` (lines 92-108) picks only from entries that were observed. The MNAR weight is `expit((q25_obs - x)/(0.5*sd_obs))`, so every masked value lies inside the observed range and above the detection limit.
- **Which proteins are scored.** Only proteins observed in at least 50% of the 30-cell subsample can be masked (`/home/user/knowledgeispower/benchmarks/panel_v9.py:56`). In `results/v9/addendum/derks2022.json` only 538 of 1093 proteins carry masked entries. The proteins with most of the real NaNs are never scored.
- **The masks ignore how data go missing in practice.** Entries are drawn independently. Real missingness has structure:
  - per-cell depth (cell size, and the 19 prep variants in karagach);
  - per-run identification failure;
  - in plexDIA/mTRAQ, all channels of a run share precursor identification;
  - in DDA, precursor selection is stochastic and depends on intensity rank.
- **No DDA or TMT data among the primary holdouts.** derks2022 is Q-Exactive plexDIA; the other two projects are timsTOF diaPASEF or Slice-PASEF.
- **Left-censored methods are penalised by construction.** On derks2022 MCAR, QRILC scores RMSE 5.37 and Perseus 3.60, against 0.92 for the champion. `docs/v9_review.md` already concedes this.
- **The mask simulator can be learned.**
  - `revised` picks ψ on a 50/50 MCAR/MNAR inner mask from the same generator (`src/scp_graphfs_mcp/phasec/cshrink.py:14-15`).
  - Its MNAR margins over the champion are about twice its MCAR margins: karagach −6.0 vs −3.2%, MDAfix −6.1 vs −3.1%, derks −3.0 vs −1.2%.
  - In Phase C, `selmnar` scored 0.877 on MNAR and 1.272 on MCAR (`docs/EXPLORATION_LOG.md`, round 3).

**What would answer it:**
- **(a) Pattern-transplant masks:** copy a real cell's NaN pattern onto another cell and score the entries that the second cell observed. This keeps per-cell depth and per-protein detectability.
- **(b) Run or plex block masks** for TMT and plexDIA data.
- **(c) Error broken down by protein detection rate and intensity decile.**
- **(d) Truth for values that are really missing.** `docs/holdout_v9_datasets.md` notes that the PXD061710 builders dropped the 2-, 5-, 10- and 50-cell runs. Those runs could check the mean imputed level of proteins that are missing in single cells.

**Can it be done from saved results?** Only (c), and only partly:
- `data/cache/v9_addendum/v3/*.npz` holds per-entry squared errors with cell and protein coordinates.
- Detection rate and intensity have to be read from the matrix. On dev splits that is allowed; on holdouts the main session would need to do it, post hoc.
- Only squared errors are stored, so signed bias cannot be recovered.
- (a), (b) and (d) need new runs. They are allowed on dev; on holdouts they are post hoc.

### 2. 30-cell random subsamples are not representative, and they inflate the value of the reference.

**Evidence:**
- **The champion is basically the reference projection here.** Low-rank alone at 30 cells is 1.24-1.36× the champion's RMSE (`docs/v9_results.md`, full panel). On karagach and the three px061710 sets, the champion's stack gives the adapted projection a weight of 0.88-1.00 (`stack_weights` in `results/confirm_v9/*.json`).
- **Gains shrink with more cells.** In Phase A, BIM roughly equals the kNN + low-rank stack at 200 cells (EXPLORATION_LOG, Amendment 13).
- **The 10 seeds are not independent replicates.** Two 30-cell draws from 76 cells share about 30·30/76 ≈ 12 cells (about 39%). From 125 cells (derks) they share about 7. The split-level bootstrap (n = 10) treats them as independent.
- **Composition is random and thin.** karagach S1 gives about 1.6 cells per prep variant per subsample, and there is no stratification.

**What would answer it:**

## Claims that survive, worded as I would accept them

**1. Reference transfer works in this setting.**
- **Scope:** 30-cell random subsamples of five matrices from three DIA projects (four are single cultured lines with technical prep or fixation contrasts), scored on simulated masks of detected values in proteins seen in at least 50% of cells.
- **Method:** the champion stacks kNN, low-rank and an adapted projection onto loadings learned from about 12,000 public single-cell profiles.
- **Result:** it reduced masked-entry RMSE in every holdout × mask:
  - by 3.0-14.0% vs the kNN + low-rank stack;
  - by 2.7-4.1% vs the same reference with proteins permuted;
  - by 2.6-8.3% vs no reference.
- **Reading:** protein identity in the reference matters.
- **Caveat:** cluster-bootstrap robustness is confirmed so far only for derks2022. The other holdouts are still running in the addendum.

**2. The champion did not beat the strongest data-only method in the panel.**
- H16 was not confirmed (1 of 3 projects).
- Under MCAR, the champion was not significantly better than the edge-free masked MLP (`gcn_nograph+stack`) on 4 of 5 matrices, and had higher RMSE on 3 of them.
- On derks2022, a correctly oriented data-only BPCA beat it.

**3. The `cshrink` revision lowered RMSE relative to the champion everywhere, with qualifications.**
- It did so on all 5 matrices × 2 masks, by 1.2-6.1%: H17 confirmed as preregistered.
- On derks2022 it fails the strict SESOI reading (2/4).
- Its MNAR margins are partly tuned to the mask simulator.
- I would not claim more than that the revision improves on the champion under these masks.

**4. "Beats the strongest typical methods" is not supported.**
- H18 failed (1 of 3 projects).
- On derks2022, `revised` is worse than or tied with data-only BPCA.
- The panel has no dedicated single-cell proteomics imputer beyond the PIMMS attempt (PIMMS CF/VAE were added post hoc and did not beat the champion on derks). It also has no R tools (msImpute, omicsGMF) and no Lupine.

**5. Graph priors did not help over no graph.**
- In this 2-layer GCN, STRING edges beat a degree-preserving shuffle but lost to the same network with no edges on every holdout and mask.
- There is no evidence that a generic PPI graph helps over data alone here.
- v9 offers no evidence for curated complex membership. Phase A-C found it adds nothing measurable once an empirical reference is used.

**Not established for any method:** real (natural) missing values, values below the detection limit, proteins detected in fewer than 50% of cells, DDA or TMT holdouts, primary tissue, cohorts larger than 30 cells, and any downstream analysis (differential expression, clustering, correlation networks).

### Strongest honest one-paragraph conclusion

v9 is a well-controlled test of reference transfer, not a test of curated biological priors, and it gives no support to the original thesis. Curated complex membership was not in any v9 method; it appeared only as a scoring subset covering most entries. The one curated-knowledge graph that was tested, STRING, was consistently harmful in a GCN compared with using no graph. It only looked "informative" because a shuffled STRING was even more harmful, and that difference did not concentrate in complex members. The stacked STRING methods gained no more than a generic data-only third component. What does replicate across three new projects is a 3–8% gain from borrowing protein loadings from public single-cell proteomics data, compared with permuted or absent loadings. That is an empirical, data-derived prior. Its permutation null cannot tell biological co-variation apart from per-protein scale. Its edge over the best data-only methods is unresolved: H16 passed on 1 of 3 projects, and a correctly implemented BPCA beat it on derks2022. The most robust v9 improvement (H17) came from a data-only change to standardisation. After nine phases, the defensible statement is that public SCP data carries transferable protein-specific information. No test so far shows that curated biological knowledge, complexes in particular, improves single-cell proteomics imputation by a meaningful margin.
